newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian troops freed; cleric sees hope for peace.
newsitem.headline: Colombian troops freed; cleric sees hope for peace.

text.p: Leftist rebels swept into this remote jungle town on Sunday and ended Latin America's longest-running hostage crisis by releasing 70 soldiers and marines they took prisoner months ago.

Mothers and sons wept as they were reunited in the central square under the gaze of some 200 heavily armed guerrillas and thousands of onlookers. The Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) seized 60 soldiers in fighting more than nine months ago and 10 marines in combat last January.
Roman Catholic Church leaders involved in arranging the release of the troops believe the handover may open the door to eventual talks aimed at ending Colombia's three-decade-old uprising.

Cmdr. Joaquin Gomez, head of the FARC's so-called Southern Bloc, called at the ceremony for the country to strive for peace with social justice. But army commander Gen. Manuel Jose Bonett vowed to hunt the rebels down once this swathe of the southern province of Caqueta was remilitarized on June 23.

"We will continue as we have always done, fighting tirelessly for peace with social justice, convinced that the struggle will always be relevant in Colombia," Gomez said as the crowd applauded and a committee of international delegates, including former Costa Rican President Rodrigo Carazo, watched.
"The FARC have always expressed their will for a social and political solution to the conflict and believe we can only do that by uniting all strands of civil society," Gomez added.

The FARC's Aug. 30, 1996, attack on the Las Delicias military base in neighbouring Putumayo province, in which the 60 soldiers were captured and some 30 others were killed, was one of the most humiliating defeats for the army in the long history of Colombia's internal war.

Political analysts said the FARC also scored one of its most important political triumphs by forcing the army to pull out of a 5,000-square-mile (13,000-sq km) jungle zone for 32 days to make way for the troop release. It was the first time the military had ceded such a large area to the rebels.

"This is a spectacular public relations and even diplomatic triumph for the FARC, who will only increase their armed belligerance," Enrique Santos wrote in his Sunday column in the leading newspaper El Tiempo.
But in interviews with the press, the bishop of nearby San Vicente del Caguan, Augusto Castro, who played a key role in the hostage handover, said there was a ray of hope for an end to the violence.
"This (release) was an aperitif for peace that will open up an appetite for real and long-lasting peace," he said.

In a news conference just before they were formally given to their waiting mothers and representatives of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) and the National Conciliation Commission, the servicemen spoke of their time in captivity.
"The situation wasn't the best, the conditions weren't the best. We accepted that and waited with peace and courage," Pvt. Nelson Nunez said.
Few showed any bitterness toward their rebel captors. "These are ordinary people. They have one ideology, we have another," marine Alexander Sape Sanchez said.

The 70 hostages began arriving in the hardscrabble town of Cartagena del Chaira shortly after 8:30 a.m. (1330 GMT) in Russian-made helicopters loaned to the ICRC by the Colombian army. They had been transported from an undisclosed location in the jungle.
